question: Your organization has three related projects (API, frontend, shared utilities) that are tightly coupled. Should you use a monorepo or separate repositories, and what are the trade-offs?
options: Monorepo simplifies cross-project changes and dependency management but requires discipline in structure and CI configuration; separate repos isolate changes but complicate shared dependencies
Always use monorepo
Always use separate repositories
It makes no difference
explanation: Monorepos excel with tightly-coupled projects; separate repos work better for independent projects with different release cycles.

question: Your repository has a vendor/ directory containing third-party code that is frequently updated. You want to track it in Git but easily distinguish it from your own code for reviews. What approach should you use?
options: Use git subtree or git submodule to link the third-party repository separately; this isolates their history from yours and simplifies updates
Commit vendor code directly with your code
Delete vendor code and add a note to install it manually
Use symlinks to reference external code
explanation: Subtree and submodule integrate external repositories while keeping their history separate; updates can be pulled independently.

question: Your team uses a branching model with main (stable), develop (integration), and short-lived feature branches. A critical bug is discovered in production (main). How should you apply the fix using this model?
options: Create a hotfix branch from main, fix and merge back to main, then merge main back to develop to keep histories in sync
Apply the fix to develop first, then merge to main
Create a separate emergency branch
Modify main directly without branching
explanation: Hotfix branches handle production emergencies; merging both directions ensures the fix reaches all active branches and prevents regression when develop is next merged.

question: Your repository root is cluttered with configuration files (package.json, tsconfig.json, .eslintrc, Dockerfile, etc.). Should these be organized into subdirectories, and what are the implications?
options: Root-level config files are conventional and easier for tools to discover; moving them to subdirectories requires adjusting tool configurations and breaking conventions, only do this if you have many configs and clear organization need
Always move config to subdirectories
Config location does not matter
Spread configs across the project randomly
explanation: Tools expect config files in the root (e.g., package.json); moving them requires explicit configuration in tool invocations or environment variables.

question: Your project has a large /docs directory (100MB) that is rarely accessed. Should it be in the same Git repository as the code, or should you separate it?
options: Keep it separate (git submodule or separate repo) if docs have independent release cycles, different teams, or rarely accessed; keep it together if docs are tightly coupled with code and always deployed together
Always keep docs in the main repository
Always separate docs into a different repository
Size alone should determine separation
explanation: Separation makes sense when release cycles differ; coupling makes sense when docs evolve with code.

question: You are setting up a repository for a multi-platform mobile app (iOS, Android, web) developed by separate teams. Should this be one repository or three separate ones?
options: One monorepo with clear directory structure (ios/, android/, web/) and separate CI pipelines per platform enables shared code/utilities while maintaining independent builds and deployments
Always use a monorepo
Always use separate repositories
Platform is irrelevant to repository structure
explanation: Monorepo with platform isolation balances code sharing and team independence; the choice depends on whether platforms share code or release independently.

question: Your repository has a src/ directory with application code and a tests/ directory with separate tests. A reviewer suggests co-locating tests with source files (e.g., src/module.js and src/module.test.js). What are the trade-offs?
options: Co-location improves maintainability (tests stay with code) but complicates production builds (excluding tests); separate directories isolate tests and simplify builds but risk tests drifting from code
Co-location is always better
Separate directories are always better
There is no difference
explanation: Co-location pairs tests with code logically; production builds must explicitly exclude .test.js files to avoid shipping tests.

question: Your team is adopting trunk-based development (all work on main) instead of long-lived branches. What infrastructure and practices are essential to make this safe?
options: Require strong CI/CD (automated tests, fast feedback), feature flags to hide incomplete work, and frequent (daily) deployments to catch issues early
Just push to main without checks
Long-lived branches are mandatory
No infrastructure changes are needed
explanation: Trunk-based development requires rapid feedback loops (CI) and feature flags to isolate work; without these, main becomes unstable.

question: Your open-source project is hosted on GitHub. You want to encourage external contributions while maintaining code quality. What repository structure should you establish?
options: Maintain clear CONTRIBUTING.md with setup instructions, branching guidelines, and PR checklist; enforce code review and CI; have a CODEOWNERS file to route reviews; label issues for new contributors
Accept all PRs without review
Reject contributions from outsiders
Repository structure does not matter for OSS
explanation: Open repositories require clear documentation and process; CODEOWNERS and issue labels reduce friction for contributors.

question: You inherit a repository with 10 years of history, 500GB of Git objects (mostly old binaries), and hundreds of unused branches. What is the best approach to modernize it?
options: Use git filter-repo to remove old binaries from history, prune unused branches with git branch -D, run git gc --aggressive, then document the cleanup in the README
Recreate the repository from scratch
Leave it as-is since changing it is risky
Delete the repository and restart
explanation: filter-repo cleans history safely; pruning and gc reduce size; documentation preserves the history of cleanup for future developers.
